title: Day and night: why the Sun seems to move across the sky
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Primary Science Stage 2, Unit 5.3 'The Sun appears to move!' (the Sun as our light source, its apparent path from east to west, shadows through the day). No textbook needed.
summary: The Sun seems to cross the sky every day, but it is really our Earth that turns. Your child watches the Sun rise in the east, climb high at midday and set in the west. They chase their own shadows, track a shadow stick through a whole day, make a paper-plate sundial, and meet the plants and animals that keep time by the Sun: flowers that open and close, leaves that 'sleep', owls and bats that wake when we go to bed.
builds_on: This is the first rung. In Class 4 your child will spin a globe in front of a lamp to see exactly why day and night happen and why sunrise comes earlier in Arunachal than in Gujarat. In Class 5 they will tilt the globe to find out why we have seasons, and meet the body clocks of birds, plants and people.
goals: By the end your child can say that the Sun rises in the east, is highest around midday and sets in the west, and point to these directions from home.
By the end your child can explain that the Sun only appears to move, because the Earth is turning, using their own body as a model.
By the end your child can predict where a shadow will fall and say why shadows are long in the morning and evening and short at midday.
By the end your child can use a shadow to tell roughly what time of day it is, and make a simple sundial.
By the end your child can name animals and plants that are active by day and by night, and say how they 'know' the time.

days.title: Where is the Sun right now?
days.goal: Notice the Sun's place in the sky and learn the safe way to watch it.

steps.title: Sunlight in our home
steps.do: Ask: 'In the morning, which room does the sunlight come into first? Which window gets the evening sun?' Walk to those windows together. Good answers: 'the kitchen gets morning sun', 'the balcony gets evening sun'. Say: 'That is a clue. The Sun is in a different place in the morning and the evening. This week we are going to find out where it goes.'

steps.title: The one big safety rule
steps.do: Say firmly but calmly: 'The Sun is so bright that looking straight at it can hurt your eyes, and the harm can last for ever. We never look straight at it, not even with sunglasses. We look at where it is by looking at the sky near it, or at shadows.' Ask your child to repeat the rule back. Show the safe way: stand with your back to the Sun and look at your shadow, or hold up a hand to block the Sun and look at the sky beside it.

steps.title: Mark the morning Sun
steps.do: Do Activity a1, part 1. Between 8 and 9 am, go to a window, balcony or terrace where you can see the sky. Mark a spot to stand on with chalk. Your child points to where the Sun is, without looking straight at it, and says which tree, building or water tank it is above. Draw the view with a small Sun in its place. Use a phone compass to check that this is east, and write 'EAST' on the drawing.

steps.title: Story: Selvi's Shadow Knows the Way
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Stop after Selvi loses sight of the herd and ask: 'How could she find her way home with nobody to ask?' Let them guess. Finish the story. Ask the story questions about why Selvi walked towards the setting Sun.

steps.title: Make a prediction
steps.do: Ask: 'Where do you think the Sun will be at lunchtime? And just before dark?' Write down their guess on the a1 sheet. Good answers: 'higher up', 'over the other side'. Do not correct yet: we will test it.

steps.title: Sunrise and sunset song
steps.do: Make up a call-and-response song together. You sing 'Where is the Sun in the morning?' and your child sings back 'Low in the east, low in the east!' Then 'Where is the Sun at midday?' ('High up above!') and 'Where is the Sun in the evening?' ('Low in the west!'). Your child points the right way each time. Sing it again on later days.

need: a phone compass if you have one

days.title: Making shadows
days.goal: Find out what a shadow is and how the light's place changes it.

steps.title: Check yesterday's guess
steps.do: At lunchtime (or as near as you can), go back to the chalk spot. Is the Sun higher? Is it above a different thing? Add the midday Sun to the a1 drawing. Ask: 'Was your guess right?'

steps.title: What is a shadow?
steps.do: In a dim room, shine a torch at a wall and put your hand in the beam. Ask: 'Why is there a dark shape?' Good answer: 'My hand stops the light, so no light reaches the wall there.' Try a steel glass, a plastic bottle of water and a sheet of paper. Ask: 'Which one lets some light through?' Say: 'A shadow is the place where light can't reach.'

steps.title: Torch high, torch low
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Your child moves the torch like the Sun from 'sunrise' (low on one side) over the top to 'sunset' (low on the other side), while you trace the shadow of a toy at each place.

steps.title: Shadow tag and shadow dance
steps.do: Go to a sunny terrace, compound or park. Play shadow tag: you are 'out' if someone steps on your shadow. Afterwards ask: 'How did you keep your shadow safe?' Good answers: 'I stood in the shade so I had no shadow', 'I faced the Sun so my shadow was behind me'. Then put on music and let your child dance with their shadow: make it tall (arms up), tiny (curl into a ball), and make it touch a friend's shadow without your bodies touching.

steps.title: Shadow rule
steps.do: Ask your child to finish the sentence: 'My shadow is always on the side ____ from the Sun.' (away)

need: a steel glass, a water bottle, paper

days.title: A day of shadows
days.goal: Track one shadow through a whole day and find the pattern.

steps.title: Set up the shadow stick
steps.do: Do Experiment e2 in the morning: push a stick upright into a pot of soil or a lump of clay. Put it on the sunniest spot you have: a terrace, a balcony or a window sill. If the Sun leaves your spot, mark as many times as you can. Mark the end of the shadow with a stone or chalk and write the time.

steps.title: Shadow checks through the day
steps.do: Every two hours (about 9, 11, 1, 3, 5) go out for two minutes. Mark the end of the shadow and write the time beside it. Each time ask: 'Is the shadow longer or shorter than last time? Which way did it move?' Also add the afternoon Sun to the a1 drawing at about 4 pm.

steps.title: Read the shadow pattern
steps.do: At the end of the day, look at the chalk marks together. Ask: 'When was the shadow longest? Shortest? Which way did it point in the morning, and in the evening?' Good answers: 'long in the morning and evening, short at lunchtime', 'it pointed west in the morning and east in the evening'. Ask: 'Why?' Good answer: 'The Sun was low then, and high at midday', 'The shadow is always on the side away from the Sun.'

steps.title: Draw it
steps.do: Your child draws the stick with three shadows: morning, midday, evening, and a little Sun in the right place for each. Check: the Sun and its shadow must be on opposite sides of the stick.

need: a pot of soil or a lump of clay

days.title: Is the Sun moving, or are we?
days.goal: Use our own bodies to see that the Earth turns and the Sun only seems to move.

steps.title: Trees that run backwards
steps.do: Ask: 'When you are in a bus or train, and you look out of the window, what do the trees seem to do?' Good answer: 'They seem to rush backwards.' Ask: 'Are the trees really moving?' (No, we are.) Say: 'Hold on to that idea. Today it will help us with the Sun.'

steps.title: Be the Earth
steps.do: Do Activity a2. Put a lamp (the Sun) in the middle of the room. Your child is the Earth and their nose is their home. They turn slowly on the spot, anticlockwise, and call out 'sunrise!', 'midday!', 'sunset!' and 'night!' as the lamp comes into view, is in front of them, goes out of view, and is behind them.

steps.title: Aryabhata and the boat
steps.do: Tell your child about Voice v1, Aryabhata, who said about 1,500 years ago that the Earth turns. Read his boat idea slowly: 'A person in a moving boat sees the trees on the bank moving backwards. In the same way the stars, which do not move, seem to move west.' Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Say it in one line
steps.do: Ask: 'Why does the Sun seem to walk across the sky?' Help your child make one sentence: 'Our Earth turns, so the Sun seems to move from east to west.' Ask them to teach this to someone else at home tonight, using the lamp.

steps.title: Drama: who is moving?
steps.do: Act a two-minute play. You are the Sun, standing proudly still with a torch. Your child is the Earth, spinning slowly. The Earth says: 'Sun, why do you keep walking across my sky?' The Sun says: 'I haven't moved a step! Look at your own feet.' The Earth spins, notices, and says the last line in their own words. Swap parts and play it again.

need: a lamp without its shade, or a bright torch on a table

days.title: Who wakes at night?
days.goal: Find out that animals, plants and our own bodies follow the rhythm of day and night.

steps.title: Day jobs and night jobs
steps.do: Ask: 'Which people in our town work at night?' (watchman, nurse, baker, train driver). 'Which animals do you hear at night?' (crickets, owls, frogs, geckos). Say: 'Some animals are diurnal, awake in the day. Some are nocturnal, awake at night.'

steps.title: Day or night animal sort
steps.do: Do section A of the core worksheet ws1 together: sort sparrow, owl, bat, butterfly, cow, firefly, squirrel, gecko into day and night. For each night animal ask: 'How do they find their way in the dark?' (Owls have huge eyes and sharp ears. Many small bats send out squeaks and listen for the echo. Fireflies make their own light.)

steps.title: Flowers that keep time
steps.do: Tell your child about Voice v2, Carl Linnaeus and his flower clock. Talk about flowers they may know. Parijat (pavazha malli in Tamil) opens at night and drops its flowers at dawn. The four o'clock flower (andhi mandharai in Tamil) opens in the late afternoon. The lotus opens in the morning. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Do leaves sleep?
steps.do: Do Experiment e3. Find a plant whose leaves fold at night: a tamarind (puli) or rain tree on your street, a touch-me-not, or the small three-leaved wood sorrel weed that grows in many flower pots. Look at it in daylight and photograph or draw it. Look again after dark with a torch.

steps.title: My body clock
steps.do: Ask: 'When do you start feeling sleepy? Do you wake up at the same time even without an alarm?' Say: 'Inside you there is a body clock that knows day from night, just like the plants and owls.'

need: a plant whose leaves fold at night

days.title: Telling time by the Sun
days.goal: Make a sundial and use shadows as a clock.

steps.title: Surya Namaskar facing east
steps.do: If you can, do this at sunrise; otherwise in the morning. Stand facing east (find it from your chalk mark) and do three slow rounds of Surya Namaskar together, breathing in as you stretch up and out as you bend. Remind your child to look at the ground and the sky near the Sun, never at the Sun itself. Ask: 'Which way are you facing? Where will the Sun be when you do this in the evening?' (Behind you, in the west.)

steps.title: Check the sleepy leaves
steps.do: Look at the e3 drawings. Ask: 'Were the leaves folded at night? Why might a plant fold their leaves?' Ideas to listen for: 'to keep warm', 'to keep dew off', 'to rest'. Say: 'Scientists still argue about why. Nobody is sure.'

steps.title: Make a paper-plate sundial
steps.do: Do Activity a3. Push a pencil through the middle of a paper plate, set it on a sunny spot, and mark the shadow every hour that you can today. Write the time on each line.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Your child does the stretch worksheet ws2. Read each question aloud if needed. For the 'why' questions, let them talk first, then write one sentence.

steps.title: The Sun's Journey
steps.do: Play a first round of the board game g1 (the Sun's Journey). Keep the board for Day 7.

need: a lump of clay to hold the plate down
the printed game board, a die and counters

days.title: Sun diary poster, check and teach it back
days.goal: Put the week together and teach it to someone else.

steps.title: Finish the Sun-path poster
steps.do: Finish the project: stick the three Sun drawings from a1 on one big sheet in a curve from east to west, with the sundial marks and shadow-stick drawing below. Your child labels sunrise, midday and sunset, and draws an arrow saying 'The Earth turns this way.'

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Your child tries the challenge worksheet ws3. Talk through the 'what if' questions together. Some have no single right answer, so listen for reasons.

steps.title: End check
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud. Praise reasons, not just answers. For any wrong answer, go back to the lamp and spin again.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches a grandparent or sibling, using the lamp and their own body: 'The Sun stays still. The Earth turns. That's why the Sun seems to walk across the sky, and why my shadow moves.' The listener asks one question and your child answers it.

experiments.title: Torch high, torch low
experiments.question: How does the place of the light change a shadow?
steps: Stand the toy on the paper in a dim room.
Hold the torch low on the right side (sunrise). Trace the shadow.
Hold it halfway up, then straight above (midday). Trace each shadow.
Move it halfway down and then low on the left (sunset). Trace each shadow.
Number the shadows 1 to 5.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: 'Will the shadow be longer when the torch is low or high? Which way will it point?'
experiments.observe: Low torch: long shadow pointing away from the torch. Torch overhead: tiny shadow right under the toy. The shadow swings round from one side to the other.
experiments.why: Light travels in straight lines. When the light comes from low down, the toy blocks a long strip of it, so the shadow is long. When the light comes from above, the toy blocks only a little patch under itself. The real Sun does the same: low in the morning and evening, high at midday.
experiments.safety: Do not shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

experiments.title: A day of shadows
experiments.question: How does a shadow change through a whole day?
need: a pot of soil or lump of clay
steps: In the morning, push the stick straight up into the soil on a spot that stays sunny all day.
Mark the tip of the shadow with chalk or a stone and write the time.
Repeat every two hours until late afternoon.
Do not move the stick or the pot.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Where will the shadow be at lunchtime? Will it be longer or shorter?'
experiments.observe: The shadow starts long and pointing west, gets shorter until around midday, then grows long again pointing east. The marks make a curve.
experiments.why: The Sun seems to move from east to west, so the shadow, which is always on the side away from the Sun, swings from west to east. The Sun is highest around midday, so the shadow is shortest then. The real reason the Sun 'moves' is that the Earth is turning.
experiments.safety: Never look straight at the Sun while you do this.
experiments.time: 10 min to set up + 2 min every 2 hours

experiments.title: Do leaves sleep?
experiments.question: Do some plants change their leaves between day and night?
need: a tamarind, rain tree, touch-me-not or wood sorrel plant
paper and crayons or a phone camera
steps: In daylight, draw or photograph a few leaves of the plant.
After dark, go back with a grown-up and a torch. Look at the same leaves.
Draw or photograph them again.
If you can, look once more early next morning.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'Will the leaves look the same at night?'
experiments.observe: These plants fold their small leaflets together at night and open them in the morning.
experiments.why: Plants that fold their leaves at night are showing 'sleep movements'. They are partly answering the light and partly following their own inner clock: in 1729 a French scientist, Jean-Jacques de Mairan, kept a touch-me-not plant in a dark cupboard, and their leaves still opened and closed on time. Why plants do it is still debated: it may save heat or keep water off the leaves.
experiments.safety: A grown-up must come along after dark. Touch-me-not has small prickles: look, don't grab.
experiments.time: 5 min in the day + 5 min after dark

activities.title: Where is the Sun? A sky diary
steps: Choose one spot to stand on and mark it with chalk.
In the morning, draw the view in front of you and a small Sun where it is (don't look at it directly).
At lunchtime and in the late afternoon, stand on the same spot and draw the Sun again.
Write the time under each drawing.
Join the three Suns with a curved line.
activities.outcome: Three drawings showing the Sun low in the east, high at midday and low in the west: the path the Sun seems to walk every day.

activities.title: Be the Earth
need: a lamp or torch in the middle of the room
steps: The lamp is the Sun. Your child is the Earth; their nose is their home.
They turn slowly on the spot, anticlockwise (to their left).
When the lamp first comes into the corner of their eye, they call 'sunrise!'
When it is right in front of them: 'midday!' When it disappears: 'sunset!' When it is behind them: 'night!'
Ask: 'Did the lamp move? What moved?'
activities.outcome: Your child feels in their own body that turning makes the Sun seem to rise, cross and set.

activities.title: Paper-plate sundial
steps: Push the pencil through the centre of the plate so it stands up straight.
Stick the plate on a flat sunny spot with clay so it can't move.
On the hour, draw a line along the pencil's shadow and write the time.
On the next sunny days, put it in the same place and the same way round. Now it tells the time.
activities.outcome: A working sundial, and the idea that people told time by shadows long before clocks.

project.title: My Sun-path poster
steps: Keep the three a1 drawings of the Sun in the morning, midday and evening.
Add the drawing of the shadow stick with its marks from Day 3.
Add the sundial times from Day 6.
Stick them in order on one big sheet in a curve from east to west.
Label east, west, sunrise, midday, sunset, and draw an arrow: 'The Earth turns this way'.
project.outcome: A poster that shows the Sun's daily path and the shadows it makes, made from your child's own observations.

game.title: The Sun's Journey
rules: Roll and move. If you land on a question square, answer it. A right answer moves you on 1 more.
If you land on 'Looked at the Sun!', go back to START.
The first to reach NIGHT wins, and must say why it is night.
squares: Which way does the Sun rise?
Where does your shadow point now?
Looked at the Sun! Back to start
Is the Sun moving? What is?
Midday heat: rest in the shade, miss a turn
Four o'clock flower opens: move on 1
Clouds! No shadow, miss a turn
Sundial time: say the time of day
Sunset in the west: move on 1

big: If you lived on a planet that never turned, what would your life be like?
Is it 'morning' for the whole world at the same time?
Why do you think some animals chose the night?
Before clocks, people told time by the Sun. Was that better or worse than a clock?

challenge.q: Everyone says 'The Sun rises in the east.' Does it rise exactly in the east every day?
challenge.hint: Only on two days a year, around 21 March and 23 September. In June it rises to the north of east. In December it rises to the south of east. Mark where the Sun rises from your window once a month and see for yourself.

challenge.q: 'Sunflowers follow the Sun all day.' Is that true?
challenge.hint: Partly. Young sunflower plants do turn from east to west during the day, and swing back at night. In 2016 scientists showed that the plants' own inner clock helps. But once the flower is fully open, the plant stops turning and faces east. What would you need to watch to check this yourself?

challenge.q: 'At midday the Sun is right above your head.' Is it?
challenge.hint: Not usually. In southern India the midday Sun is exactly overhead on only two days a year, called Zero Shadow Days. In Bengaluru they come in late April and mid August. On those days, for a moment, an upright stick has no shadow. In northern cities such as Delhi, the Sun is never exactly overhead.

perspectives.view: For an owl, our day is the quiet sleeping time, and the dark is the busy time for hunting rats and mice. Ask: whose clock is the 'right' one, ours or the owl's?
Before clocks were common, many farmers told the time of day by the length of their own shadow. Ask: what can they see that someone indoors with a clock might miss?

In many traditions, prayers follow the Sun. Hindu Sandhya prayers are said at dawn and dusk. One of the five Muslim daily prayers, Asr, begins when a shadow has grown to a set length. Ask: why might people stop to pray at sunrise and sunset?

voices.who: Aryabhata (476–about 550 CE), Kusumapura, near present-day Patna, India
voices.idea: In his book the Aryabhatiya (499 CE) he wrote that the Earth turns on its own, and that the stars only seem to move west, just as trees on a river bank seem to move backwards to a person in a moving boat.
voices.then: Many later Indian astronomers, including Brahmagupta, did not accept that the Earth turns.
voices.now: Aryabhata was right: the Earth turns once a day. In 1851 Léon Foucault showed it clearly with a long swinging pendulum in Paris.
voices.ask: If the Earth is spinning, why don't we feel it? What could you look for to show that it really turns?

voices.idea: In 1751 he described a 'flower clock': a garden of flowers that open and close at different hours, so you could tell the time by which ones were open.
voices.then: People loved the idea and tried planting such clocks.
voices.now: Many flowers do open and close at regular times, partly because of light and partly because of their own inner clocks. But gardeners who planted flower clocks found they worked only roughly, because flowers change their times with weather, season and place.
voices.ask: If a flower opens at 6 am in Sweden, would it open at 6 am in Chennai too? How could you find out?

books.title: Sun Up, Sun Down
books.author: Gail Gibbons
books.why: A girl follows the Sun from sunrise to sunset, with shadows, clouds and the turning Earth explained in simple pictures.

books.title: What Makes Day and Night
books.author: Franklyn M. Branley
books.why: A classic Let's-Read-and-Find-Out book that uses a lamp and a ball, just like our Activity a2.

books.title: Moonbear's Shadow
books.author: Frank Asch
books.why: A bear tries to get rid of his shadow, and finds that it changes with the time of day: funny, and good science.

books.title: Shadow
books.author: Suzy Lee
books.why: A wordless book in which a girl's shadow play in an attic comes alive. Good for talking about how shadows are made.

check.q: Where does the Sun rise and where does it set?
check.a: It rises in the east and sets in the west.

check.q: Does the Sun really move across the sky?
check.a: No. The Earth turns, so the Sun only seems to move.

check.q: When is your shadow shortest, and why?
check.a: Around midday, because the Sun is highest in the sky.

check.q: In the morning, which way does your shadow point?
check.a: West, away from the Sun in the east.

check.q: How does a sundial tell the time?
check.a: The shadow of its stick moves round as the Sun seems to move, so where the shadow falls shows the time.

check.q: Name one animal that is awake at night, and one plant that changes at night.
check.a: For example, owl, bat, gecko or firefly; parijat flowers open at night, tamarind leaves fold up.

check.q: What is the most important safety rule for watching the Sun?
check.a: Never look straight at it, not even with sunglasses.

story.title: Selvi's Shadow Knows the Way
text: I am Selvi's shadow. I have been with her since the day she was born, though she did not notice me until she was four. Now she is six, and most days she wishes I would go away.

"Stop copying me," she says, when I lift my arm as she lifts hers. "Stop following me," she says, when I run along the sand behind her. But I cannot stop. I go where the light cannot go. Wherever Selvi blocks the Sun, there I am.

Selvi lives in a village at the edge of the Theri, the red sand dunes in the south of Tamil Nadu. The sand is the colour of brick, and the sky is so big it makes you feel very small. Her family keeps goats. Every morning, when the Sun has just climbed out of the earth, Selvi and her grandfather and their dog Karuppu take the goats east to the grazing ground beyond the dunes, where the palmyra palms grow.

In the mornings I am very long. Selvi walks towards the Sun, and I stretch out behind her all the way back towards the village, thin as a rope, longer than three Selvis. "Look, Thatha," she says, "my shadow is holding on to the house."
"Then it knows the way home," says Thatha, and laughs his crackly laugh.

By the middle of the day, the Sun is high up over our heads, white and fierce. Then I shrink. I curl up into a small dark puddle around Selvi's feet, and she has to look down to find me. The goats lie in the thin shade of the palmyra palms, and Selvi sits with Thatha drinking kambu koozh, a millet drink, with a small onion, and I hide under her, keeping cool.
"Where did you go?" she asks me, poking at the dark patch with her toe. "Are you scared of the Sun?"
I am not scared of the Sun. I simply go to the other side of things from it. When it is low, I am long. When it is high, I am small. This is all I know, and all I do. But Selvi does not know it yet.

One afternoon, a goat called Kutty went missing. She was the youngest, a brown kid with one white ear, and she had wandered off over a dune after a juicy bush. Thatha's knees were bad, so Selvi said, "I'll get her!" and ran off with Karuppu before he could say no.
She found Kutty quickly, chewing a thorny bush in a little hollow between two dunes. Selvi hugged her and picked her up. And then she turned round, and her heart gave a jump.

Every dune looked the same. Smooth, red, rippled, curving away on every side. She could not see the palmyra palms. She could not see Thatha. She called, and the wind took her voice away. Karuppu sat down and looked at her, as if to say, "Well? You're the one in charge."
Selvi's lip began to shake. She put Kutty down and sat on the warm sand. And that is when she noticed me.

I was long again. The Sun had travelled all the way across the sky while she was chasing goats, and now it was sinking in the west, big and orange, and I was stretching out in front of her, pointing the other way from the morning. In the morning I had pointed back towards the village. Now I was pointing towards the grazing ground, the palmyra palms, the east.
Selvi looked at me for a long time. Then she looked at the Sun, squinting, not straight at it, the way Thatha had taught her, just at the bright sky beside it.

"In the morning we walked towards the Sun to come here," she said slowly to Karuppu. "So the village is on the other side. And now the Sun is on the other side." She stood up. "The Sun is going to bed over our house."

She turned her back on me. I fell in behind her, long and thin, the way I had been in the morning, only the other way round. She picked up Kutty, and she walked towards the setting Sun, and Karuppu trotted beside her, and the dunes were orange and then pink.

She walked until she reached the top of a high dune, and there below was her village, with smoke rising from the cooking fires and the first lamps being lit. And there, coming up the path with his stick, shouting her name, was Thatha.

That night, when the Sun had gone, I went away too. I always do. In the dark there is no light to block, so there is no me. Selvi lay on her rope cot under the stars, with Kutty asleep against her legs.
"Thatha," she said, "the Sun walks across the sky every day. From there to there." She pointed east, and then west.
"It seems to," said Thatha. "Or perhaps it is us who are turning."
Selvi thought about this. Then she said, "Tomorrow I won't tell my shadow to go away." And she fell asleep. In the morning, when the Sun came up, I was there again, stretching out towards home.
story.epiphany: The Sun seems to move from east to west across the sky, and a shadow always falls on the side away from it: long and pointing west in the morning, small at midday, long and pointing east in the evening. The turn comes when Selvi, lost, sees her evening shadow pointing the opposite way to the morning, and works out that home must be towards the setting Sun. The shadow that annoyed her is the thing that gets her home.
ask: Why was the shadow so long in the morning and so small at lunchtime?
How did the shadow help Selvi find the village?
If Selvi had got lost at midday, could her shadow have helped her? Why or why not?
Where did the shadow go at night?
Thatha said, 'Perhaps it is us who are turning.' What did he mean?

ideas.idea: The Sun does not move across our sky. We turn under it.
ideas.more: Use the 'Be the Earth' spin. Every sunrise is really your part of the Earth turning to face the Sun. Every sunset is your part turning away.

ideas.idea: A shadow shows where the light is coming from.
ideas.more: Shadows always point away from the light. That is how a sundial tells the time and how Selvi found her way home.

ideas.idea: Many living things keep time with the Sun.
ideas.more: Flowers that open at dawn, leaves that fold at night, owls that wake at dusk, and your own sleepy feeling at bedtime are all following the same daily rhythm.

unknowns: Why do plants like tamarind fold their leaves at night? Scientists have ideas (to keep warm, to keep dew off, to hide from hungry animals) but nobody is sure.
Why do we need to sleep at all? Every animal with a brain seems to sleep, but scientists are still working out exactly what sleep is for.
